decks.title: Globalisation and the Indian Economy — Part 1: What Globalisation Is and What Enabled It
goals: Define globalisation as the integration of countries through trade, investment, technology and the movement of people
Explain the role of MNCs and foreign trade in integrating markets
Explain how transport and information technology enabled globalisation
Explain liberalisation of trade and investment, India's 1991 changes and the role of the WTO

slides.heading: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **what globalisation is** and the **factors that made it possible**. *These two topics are the board-exam part of this chapter.*

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what globalisation is, MNCs and investment, integration of markets, technology, and liberalisation and the WTO
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Namaste! Look at the things around you: your phone, your shoes, the fruit in your kitchen. Many of them were designed, made or grown in other countries, and many things made in India are used abroad. This deep connection between countries is called globalisation. In this part we ask what globalisation is, and what made it possible. These two topics are what the board exam tests from this chapter.

slides.heading: What is globalisation?
slides.body_md: **Globalisation** is the process of **rapid integration or interconnection** between countries.

rows: Indian medicines sold in Africa; software services for banks abroad
Money spent on factories, offices, machines
A foreign company builds a factory in Gujarat
Indian hospitals use scanners designed abroad
Nurses and engineers working abroad (limited by visas)

visual.alt: Table of the four channels of globalisation: trade in goods and services, investment, technology, and people, with an example of each

slides.narration: Globalisation means that countries are becoming closely connected, very quickly. They connect in four ways. Goods and services are traded. Companies invest in factories and offices abroad. Technology, like machines and software, moves across borders. And people move for work and study. When you answer a question on globalisation, name these four channels and give an example of each.

slides.heading: Foreign trade connects markets

nodes.label: Producers sell beyond their own country
Buyers get goods from many countries
Markets of different countries become one connected market

visual.alt: Flow: producers sell beyond their own country, buyers get goods from many countries, competition crosses borders, and markets become connected
visual.caption: Foreign trade integrates markets

slides.narration: Start with trade. Foreign trade lets producers sell beyond their own country, and lets buyers choose goods made abroad. Ratnagiri mangoes reach London; New Zealand kiwis reach Pune. Sellers from many countries now compete in the same market, so choice widens and prices tend to come closer. When markets in different countries become linked like this, we say they are integrated.

slides.heading: Quick check: mangoes and kiwis
slides.body_md: Indian mangoes are sold in London, and New Zealand kiwis in Pune. What does this show?
slides.narration: Think about what happens to markets when goods from many countries are sold side by side.

slides.heading: Multinational corporations and investment

rows: A company that owns or controls production in more than one nation
Money spent to buy assets such as land, buildings, machines and equipment
Investment made by MNCs in other countries
Close to markets, where labour and other resources are cheap, and where government policies help

visual.alt: Table defining an MNC, investment and foreign investment, and where MNCs choose to produce: near markets, with cheap labour and resources, and helpful policies

slides.narration: Multinational corporations play a big part. An MNC owns or controls production in more than one country. When it spends money on land, buildings and machines abroad, that is foreign investment. Where does an MNC set up? Close to its markets, where labour and resources are cheap, and where government policies are helpful. By investing and producing across countries, MNCs move goods, money and technology across borders.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: one product, many countries
slides.body_md: Trace an imagined electric scooter and decide what it tells us about globalisation.
bullets: Step 1 — List where each part is made: Bengaluru, South Korea, China, Germany, Hosur.
Step 2 — Identify the channels: **trade** in parts, **investment** in plants, **technology** in design and batteries.
Step 3 — Note where it is sold: India and 15 other countries.
Step 4 — Conclude: production and markets of many countries are **integrated** in one product.

headers: Part of an imagined electric scooter

visual.alt: Table of where the parts of an imagined electric scooter are made: design in Bengaluru, battery cells in South Korea, motor in China, brakes in Germany, assembly in Hosur, sold in India and 15 other countries
visual.caption: Imagined example: one product, many countries.

slides.narration: Let us read one product like a map. This imagined electric scooter is designed in Bengaluru, its battery cells come from South Korea, the motor from China and the brakes from Germany, and it is assembled in Hosur. It is then sold in sixteen countries. Trade, investment and technology are all at work in a single product. That is globalisation in one picture.

slides.heading: What moves freely, and what does not

rows: Lower import taxes; containers; WTO rules

visual.alt: Table of how freely things cross borders: goods very freely, investment freely in most sectors, technology freely, people least freely because of visas and immigration rules

slides.narration: Not everything moves equally freely. Goods cross borders very easily now, because taxes on imports are lower and transport is cheap. Investment and technology also move freely in most sectors. But people move least freely: countries control who may enter and work through visas and immigration rules. So, in today's globalisation, a phone travels more easily than the engineer who designed it.

slides.heading: Quick check: the least free
slides.body_md: Which of these has moved least freely between countries in recent globalisation?
slides.narration: Think about what you need to cross a border yourself, compared with a parcel.

slides.heading: What made globalisation possible?

nodes.label: Technology: information and communication (internet, telecom, computers)
Liberalisation of foreign trade and investment policy

visual.alt: Flow from the heading Factors that enabled globalisation to four factors: transport technology, information and communication technology, liberalisation of trade and investment policy, and WTO rules
visual.caption: Three big factors (technology counted in two parts)

slides.narration: Now the second board topic: the factors that enabled globalisation. There are three big ones. First, technology, in two parts: transport technology, which moves goods cheaply, and information and communication technology, which moves information instantly. Second, liberalisation: governments removing barriers on trade and investment. Third, international rules made through the World Trade Organisation. Let us take them one by one.

slides.heading: Factor 1: transport technology
slides.body_md: Goods are packed in **containers**, which move intact between trucks, trains and ships.

nodes.label: Factory packs goods into a container
Truck or train carries the container to port
Crane lifts it onto a ship

visual.alt: Flow of a container journey: packed at the factory, carried by truck or train, lifted onto a ship, shipped abroad, and delivered unopened to the buyer
visual.caption: Containers cut handling time and cost

slides.narration: In the past, every sack and box was loaded onto ships by hand, one at a time, and loading took weeks. Today goods are packed in standard steel containers at the factory. The container travels by truck or train, is lifted onto a ship by a crane in minutes, and reaches the buyer unopened. Along with cheaper air freight, this has cut the time and cost of moving goods across the world.

slides.heading: Factor 1: information and communication technology

rows: Software maintenance by a firm in Hyderabad
Reading of medical scans by radiologists in Chennai
Animation for a cartoon series, studio in Pune
A TV channel in the USA
Accounts and payroll by a firm in Gurugram

visual.alt: Table of four services done in India for customers abroad through information technology: software maintenance, reading medical scans, animation, and accounts and payroll

slides.narration: The second part of technology is information and communication. Computers, the internet, mobile phones and satellite links let information travel instantly. So services can now be produced in one country and delivered in another. Indian firms maintain software for foreign banks, read medical scans for hospitals abroad, make animation and keep accounts, all without anyone travelling. Firms also use these tools to coordinate production spread across countries.

slides.heading: Quick check: comics from Kochi
slides.body_md: A Kochi studio colours a comic book for a publisher in Tokyo and sends the files over the internet the same evening. Which factor makes this possible?
slides.narration: Ask what carried the work from Kochi to Tokyo. Was it a ship, a person or something else?

slides.heading: Trade barriers
slides.body_md: A **trade barrier** is a restriction on foreign trade set by the government.

rows: Limits the quantity that may be imported
Only 10,000 tonnes of edible oil a year
Imports allowed only with government approval

visual.alt: Table of three trade barriers: a tax on imports makes them dearer, a quota limits quantity, and licences require government permission, each with an imagined example

slides.narration: Before we discuss liberalisation, we need to know what a trade barrier is. It is any restriction a government puts on foreign trade. A tax on imports makes foreign goods dearer. A quota limits the quantity that may come in. A licence means imports need government permission. Governments use barriers to decide what, and how much, comes into the country, often to protect their own producers.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: how an import duty changes a price
slides.body_md: An imported lamp costs ₹1,200 before duty (imagined). Find its market price with a 25% duty and with a 5% duty.
bullets: Step 3 — Cutting the duty lowers the price by **₹240**.
Step 4 — Interpret: imports become cheaper, so buyers gain and local makers face more competition.

rows: Price of imported lamp before duty

visual.alt: Table: an imported lamp costing 1,200 rupees sells for 1,500 rupees with a 25 per cent duty and for 1,260 rupees with a 5 per cent duty
visual.caption: Imagined figures.

slides.narration: See a trade barrier in numbers. With a twenty five per cent duty, a lamp costing twelve hundred rupees sells for fifteen hundred. Cut the duty to five per cent and it sells for twelve hundred and sixty. That is two hundred and forty rupees cheaper. Buyers gain, but a local lamp maker now faces tougher competition. This is exactly the trade-off governments weigh when they liberalise.

slides.heading: Factor 2: liberalisation in India

nodes.label: 1991: barriers removed to a large extent
1995: India a founding member of the WTO
2020s: trade agreements with partners such as the UAE, Australia and the UK

visual.alt: Timeline flow: barriers after 1947 to protect young industries, liberalisation from 1991, India a founding member of the WTO in 1995, and trade agreements in the 2020s with partners such as the UAE, Australia and the UK
visual.caption: India's trade policy over time

slides.narration: Here is India's story. After independence, the government put barriers on foreign trade and investment to protect young Indian industries from foreign competition. In nineteen ninety one, it decided Indian producers were ready to compete with the world, and removed barriers to a large extent. Removing such barriers is called liberalisation. India joined the World Trade Organisation when it began in nineteen ninety five, and has recently signed new trade agreements.

slides.heading: Why protect then, why open later?
columns:
**After 1947: protection**

- Industries were just starting
- Foreign firms were bigger and more experienced
- Barriers gave Indian producers time to grow
- Imports limited to essentials such as machinery and oil

**From 1991: liberalisation**

- Indian producers judged ready to compete
- Competition expected to raise quality and efficiency
- Easier imports of machines and inputs
- Foreign investment invited in many sectors
slides.narration: Compare the two periods. After independence, Indian industries were young, and foreign firms were much stronger, so barriers gave Indian producers time to grow. By nineteen ninety one, the government felt the time had come for them to compete. It expected competition to improve quality and efficiency. In an exam, always give the reason for each policy, not just the date.

slides.heading: Quick check: a limit on oil imports
slides.body_md: A country allows only 10,000 tonnes of edible oil to be imported in a year. What is this?
slides.narration: Is this limit about the price of the imports, or the quantity?

slides.heading: Factor 3: the World Trade Organisation

rows: By setting rules for trade that members agree to follow, and settling trade disputes
More than 160 countries; India since its start in 1995
It came about at the initiative of developed countries
Developed countries keep barriers and large farm subsidies while developing countries are pressed to open up

visual.alt: Table on the World Trade Organisation: its aim, how it works, members, who started it, and the criticism that developed countries keep barriers and farm subsidies

slides.narration: The third factor is the World Trade Organisation. Its aim is to liberalise international trade, and it does this by setting rules that members agree to follow. More than one hundred and sixty countries are members. But developing countries have a complaint. Some rich countries keep their own barriers and pay large subsidies to their farmers, while pressing poorer countries to open up. So the rules are not always applied fairly.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: planning a five-mark answer on the factors
slides.body_md: *Explain the factors that have enabled globalisation.* (5 marks)
bullets: Step 1 — Split technology into **transport** and **information** technology (two points).
Step 2 — Explain **liberalisation** and give India's **1991** example (two points).
Step 3 — Add the **WTO**: its aim, and the criticism of unfair practice.
Step 4 — Each point: the factor, then **what it changed** (cost, time, barriers).

rows: Containers, cheaper air freight: less time and cost
Internet, telecom: services delivered across countries
Removal of barriers on trade and investment
Barriers removed so Indian producers compete globally
Rules to liberalise trade; criticism of unfair practice

visual.alt: Answer plan table for a five-mark question on the factors of globalisation: transport technology, information technology, liberalisation, India in 1991, and the WTO
visual.caption: One mark per point.

slides.narration: Here is a plan that earns all five marks. Split technology into two points: transport, and information technology. Then explain liberalisation, and give India's example from nineteen ninety one. End with the World Trade Organisation, its aim, and the criticism. For every factor, write what it changed: lower cost, less time, or fewer barriers. That link is what examiners reward.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Rapid integration of countries: trade, investment, technology, people
Owns or controls production in more than one nation
Producers sell abroad, buyers get foreign goods, choice widens
Containers and air freight; internet and telecom
Removing barriers such as import taxes and quotas; India from 1991
Aims to liberalise trade; criticised for unfair practice

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: globalisation, MNCs, integration of markets, technology, liberalisation and the WTO

slides.narration: Here is Part 1 in brief. Globalisation is the rapid integration of countries through trade, investment, technology and the movement of people. MNCs and foreign trade connect markets and give consumers wider choice. Three factors made it possible: technology in transport and communication, liberalisation of trade and investment, which India began in nineteen ninety one, and the rules of the World Trade Organisation.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Definition: "**rapid integration or interconnection between countries**", then the four channels.
MNC: "owns or **controls production** in **more than one nation**".
Trade barrier example: **tax on imports**; liberalisation = **removing** barriers.
India: barriers after independence to **protect young industries**; removed from **1991** to compete.
WTO: aim = **liberalise international trade**; add the **criticism** in longer answers.
Only this part (what globalisation is, and its factors) is examined in the board paper.
slides.narration: Some tips. Learn the definition word for word in your own phrasing: rapid integration or interconnection between countries. For an MNC, the key words are controls production in more than one nation. For a trade barrier, give a tax on imports as the example. For India, always pair a date with a reason. And for the WTO, state its aim, and in longer answers add the criticism of unfair practice.

decks.title: Globalisation and the Indian Economy — Part 2: Production Across Countries and Fair Globalisation (project companion)
goals: Describe how MNCs spread and interlink production across countries (interdisciplinary project topic)
Analyse the impact of globalisation on different groups in India (project topic)
Suggest ways to make globalisation fairer (project topic)

slides.heading: Project companion: globalisation at work
slides.body_md: *This part is for the **interdisciplinary project**; it is **not examined** in the board paper.*

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: how MNCs spread production, attracting investment, who gains and who loses, Indian companies abroad, fair globalisation, and planning a project
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: This part is different. It covers production across countries, the impact of globalisation and the struggle for a fair globalisation. CBSE does not test these topics in the board paper; they are assessed through your interdisciplinary project. So treat this deck as a project companion: understand the ideas, collect examples from your own town, and learn how to build a balanced argument.

slides.heading: How MNCs spread production

rows: Joint production with a local company
A foreign carmaker and an Indian firm build a plant together
An MNC buys a popular Indian snack brand
A sports brand orders jerseys from small units in Tiruppur

visual.alt: Table of three ways MNCs spread production: joint production with a local company, buying a local company, and placing large orders with small producers

slides.narration: MNCs spread their production in three common ways. They set up production jointly with a local company, sharing money and technology. They buy local companies outright, often well-known brands. Or they place large orders with small producers, for garments, footwear or sports goods, and sell the products under their own brand. Each way links production in one country with markets in many others.

slides.heading: Interlinked production: an example

nodes.label: Small processors in Kollam shell and grade cashews
An MNC buys them at a fixed price
Sold in supermarkets in Europe and the Gulf

visual.alt: Flow: small cashew processors in Kollam sell to an MNC at a fixed price, the nuts are packed under the MNC brand, and sold in supermarkets in Europe and the Gulf
visual.caption: Imagined example: interlinked production

slides.narration: Here is an imagined chain. Small cashew processors in Kollam shell and grade the nuts. An MNC buys them at a fixed price, packs them under its own brand, and sells them in supermarkets in Europe and the Gulf. The small processors get steady orders, but the price is set by the powerful buyer, and much of the final price is earned by the brand. That is interlinked production.

slides.heading: Quick check: how MNCs spread
slides.body_md: Which is a common way in which MNCs spread their production in other countries?
slides.narration: Think back to the three ways on the earlier slide.

slides.heading: How governments attract foreign investment

rows: World-class power, water, roads, transport and storage; tax benefits for some years
Payments to firms that raise production in India, e.g. mobile phones
Foreign investment allowed in most sectors

visual.alt: Table of policies to attract foreign investment: Special Economic Zones under the 2005 Act, production-linked incentives since 2020, and easier rules for foreign investment

slides.narration: Governments compete to attract MNCs. India set up Special Economic Zones, under a law of two thousand five, offering world-class power, water, roads and storage, with tax benefits for some years. Since twenty twenty, production-linked incentives reward firms that raise output in India, for example in mobile phones, and many phones sold worldwide are now made here. Rules for foreign investment have also been eased.

slides.heading: Who gains, who loses?

visual.alt: Table of the impact of globalisation on consumers, large Indian companies, small producers and workers, showing gains and losses for each

slides.narration: Globalisation has not affected everyone the same way. Consumers, especially well-off ones in cities, have more choice and better quality at lower prices. Large Indian companies gained technology, partners and new markets. But many small producers were hurt by cheaper imports. And for many workers, jobs have become more temporary and insecure. Your project should show both sides.

slides.heading: Quick check: who gained most clearly?
slides.body_md: Which group in India has generally gained most clearly from globalisation?
slides.narration: Look at the gains and losses table. Which row has gains and no clear losses?

slides.heading: Indian companies go global

rows: Bought the European steelmaker Corus in 2007
Took over mobile networks in many African countries in 2010
Offices and clients across the world

visual.alt: Table of Indian companies that went global: Tata Steel bought Corus in 2007, Bharti Airtel took over mobile networks in Africa in 2010, and Indian IT companies operate worldwide

slides.narration: Globalisation works both ways. Some Indian companies have become multinationals themselves. Tata Steel bought the European steelmaker Corus in two thousand seven. Bharti Airtel took over mobile networks in many African countries in two thousand ten. Indian IT companies have offices and clients across the world. For a project, look for a company from your own state that sells or produces abroad.

slides.heading: The hard side of globalisation
columns:
**Small producers**

- Compete with cheaper imports
- Little capital to buy new technology
- Some lose business or close
- Workers in those units lose jobs

**Workers**

- Employers seek "flexibility"
- Short contracts, long hours in peak season
- Fewer benefits, less security
- Gains not shared fairly
slides.narration: Now the hard side. Many small producers, with little capital and old machines, cannot match cheaper imports or big global brands, and some have closed. Workers face pressure too. Employers competing on cost want flexibility, which often means short contracts, long hours in peak seasons and fewer benefits. So the gains of globalisation are not shared equally.

slides.heading: Towards a fair globalisation

nodes.label: Fair globalisation: benefits shared by all
Developing countries negotiate fairer WTO rules together

visual.alt: Flow from fair globalisation to four supports: enforcing labour laws, supporting small producers, negotiating fairer WTO rules together, and people's organisations
visual.caption: Making globalisation fairer

slides.narration: How can globalisation be made fairer, so that its benefits are shared by all? The government can enforce labour laws properly, so workers get their rights. It can support small producers with credit and technology until they can compete. Developing countries can negotiate together for fairer rules at the World Trade Organisation. And people's organisations can campaign for workers and small producers.

slides.heading: Quick check: Special Economic Zones
slides.body_md: Special Economic Zones are set up to do what?
slides.narration: Recall what an SEZ offers to companies, and why.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a shop survey for your project
slides.body_md: Survey four products in a local shop (imagined results) and draw a conclusion.
bullets: Step 1 — For each product, note the **brand country** and where it was **made**.
Step 2 — Notice: a Korean phone and a Japanese washing machine are **made in India**.
Step 3 — Notice: American shoes are made in **Vietnam**; the biscuits are Indian throughout.
Step 4 — Conclude: brands and production are **spread across countries**; India is both a market and a production base.

headers: Product in a local shop (imagined survey)

visual.alt: Table from an imagined shop survey listing four products with the brand country, the place of manufacture and the price
visual.caption: Imagined survey for a project.

slides.narration: A simple shop survey makes a strong project. For each product, note where the brand is from and where it was made. In this imagined survey, the Korean phone and the Japanese washing machine were made in India, the American shoes in Vietnam, and the biscuits were Indian throughout. The conclusion: production is spread across countries, and India is both a market and a place where goods are made.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: building a balanced project
slides.body_md: Plan a project on "Who gains from globalisation in my town?"
bullets: Step 1 — Ask one clear question.
Step 2 — Collect **data**: a shop survey and short interviews with a shopkeeper, a worker and a small producer.
Step 3 — Present **gains** and **losses** with your evidence.
Step 4 — End with a **balanced judgement** and suggestions for fair globalisation.

rows: e.g. "Who gains from globalisation in my town?"
A shop survey, interviews with a shopkeeper, a worker, a small producer
Balanced conclusion with suggestions for fair globalisation

visual.alt: Plan for a project on globalisation in five sections: question, data, gains, losses and a balanced judgement with suggestions

slides.narration: Here is a plan for your project. Start with one clear question. Collect your own evidence: a shop survey, and short interviews with a shopkeeper, a worker and a small producer. Present the gains and the losses you found. End with a balanced judgement and two or three suggestions for a fairer globalisation. Original local evidence is what makes a project stand out.

sections.heading: 2. MNCs and foreign investment
sections.body_md:
A **multinational corporation (MNC)** owns or controls production in **more than one nation**. MNCs set up offices and factories where they are **close to markets**, where **labour and other resources are cheap**, and where government policies help, so that their costs fall and profits rise.

**Investment** is money spent on assets such as land, buildings, machines and equipment; investment by MNCs in other countries is **foreign investment**. By investing, producing and selling in many countries, MNCs move **goods, services, capital and technology** across borders, which makes them a major force in globalisation. A single product (a phone, a scooter) may be designed in one country, use parts from several others and be assembled in a third.

sections.body_md:
**Transport technology:** goods are packed in **containers** that move intact between trucks, trains, ships and planes, cutting handling time and port costs; bigger ships and cheaper air freight have lowered the cost of moving goods over long distances.

**Information and communication technology:** computers, the internet, mobile phones and satellite links let information travel instantly. Firms can **coordinate production** spread across countries, and **services** can be produced in one country and delivered in another: software maintenance, medical-scan reading, animation, accounting, call centres.

sections.heading: 4. Factor 2: liberalisation of foreign trade and investment policy
sections.body_md:
A **trade barrier** is a restriction on foreign trade set by the government: a **tax on imports** (tariff), a **quota** on quantity, or a licence. Governments use barriers to decide what, and how much, comes into the country.

- **After independence**, India put barriers on foreign trade and investment to **protect producers** whose industries were just starting; only essentials such as machinery, fertilisers and petroleum were imported freely.
- **From 1991**, the government decided that Indian producers should **compete with producers around the globe**, expecting competition to improve their performance. Barriers on trade and investment were **removed to a large extent**.

Removing barriers or restrictions set by the government is called **liberalisation**. With liberalisation, businesses can decide freely what to import or export. In recent years India has also signed trade agreements that cut duties with partners such as the **UAE and Australia (2022)** and the **United Kingdom (signed 2025)**.

sections.heading: 5. Factor 3: the World Trade Organisation
sections.body_md:
The **WTO** aims to **liberalise international trade**. It sets **rules** for international trade that members agree to follow, and helps settle trade disputes. It came about at the initiative of the **developed countries**; it has more than 160 members, and India has been a member since it began in **1995**.

**Criticism:** the WTO is supposed to allow free trade for all, but in practice developed countries have kept some barriers and pay **large subsidies** to their own farmers, while developing countries are pressed to remove protection. Developing countries argue for **fairer rules**.

sections.heading: 6. Project topic: production across countries, impact and fair globalisation
sections.body_md:
*Assessed through the interdisciplinary project, not the board paper.*

**How MNCs spread production:** joint production with local companies; buying local companies; large orders with small producers (garments, footwear, sports goods). Production in many countries becomes **interlinked**.

**Attracting investment:** **Special Economic Zones** (SEZ Act 2005) with world-class facilities and tax benefits; **production-linked incentives** (since 2020); easier rules for foreign investment.

**Impact on India:** consumers, especially well-off urban ones, gained **choice, quality and lower prices**; MNCs invested and created jobs; some Indian companies became **multinationals** (e.g. Tata Steel bought Corus in 2007; Bharti Airtel expanded into Africa in 2010); IT and service firms found new markets. But many **small producers** were hurt by competition, and employers' demand for **flexibility** made many jobs temporary and insecure.

**Fair globalisation** creates opportunities for all and shares the benefits better: the government should **enforce labour laws**, **support small producers**, use trade barriers where needed, and negotiate with other developing countries for **fairer WTO rules**; people's organisations also campaign for fairness.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Defining globalisation as "trade with foreign countries" only: include **investment, technology and people**.
- Defining an MNC as a company that "sells abroad": it must **own or control production** in more than one nation.
- Calling a tax on imports "liberalisation": a tax is a **barrier**; liberalisation **removes** barriers.
- Giving 1991 without the **reason** (Indian producers ready to compete), or the earlier barriers without theirs (protect young industries).
- Saying people move as freely as goods: people move **least freely**.
- Writing long answers about MNC strategies, impact or fair globalisation in the board paper: these are **project topics**.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark MCQ and assertion-reason: one correct option.
- 2 marks: two points (about 40 words); 3 marks: three points (about 60 words).
- 5 marks: five numbered points (about 120 words); for "factors", split technology into transport and IT, then liberalisation, India in 1991 and the WTO.

questions.stem_md: Globalisation is best described as

options.text_md: a policy of stopping all imports to protect local producers
the process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries
the movement of people from villages to cities within a country
the government taking over private companies

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries. The key idea is countries becoming closely and quickly connected (through trade, investment, technology and people). Stopping imports is protection, rural–urban migration is internal, and nationalisation is about ownership.

questions.stem_md: Through which of the following do countries become more closely connected in globalisation?

options.text_md: Only movement of people from poor to rich countries
Only the exchange of cultural programmes between governments
Only aid given by rich countries to poor ones
Movement of goods and services, investment, technology and people across countries

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Movement of goods and services, investment, technology and people across countries. Globalisation works through four channels: trade in goods and services, investment, technology and (to a smaller extent) people. Each of the other options names, at most, one narrow channel.

questions.stem_md: Which of these has moved **least freely** between countries in the recent wave of globalisation?

options.text_md: People
Goods
Investment
Technology

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** People. Goods, investment and technology now cross borders far more easily than before. Movement of people is still limited by visas, work permits and immigration rules.

questions.stem_md: A multinational corporation (MNC) is a company that

options.text_md: sells its goods only in its home country
is owned by the governments of several countries
owns or controls production in more than one nation
employs workers from many countries in a single factory

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** owns or controls production in more than one nation. An MNC owns or controls production (factories, offices) in more than one country. Selling only at home, government ownership, or a multinational workforce in one factory do not define it.

questions.stem_md: When a company based in South Korea spends money to buy land, build a factory and install machines in Uttar Pradesh, this is an example of

options.text_md: a trade barrier
a quota on imports
foreign investment
disguised unemployment

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** foreign investment. Investment is money spent on assets such as land, buildings and machines; when an MNC makes it in another country, it is foreign investment. Barriers and quotas restrict trade; disguised unemployment is unrelated.

questions.stem_md: Alphonso mangoes from Ratnagiri are sold in London, and kiwis from New Zealand are sold in Pune. What does this show?

options.text_md: Foreign trade is integrating markets in different countries
Both countries have banned imports of fruit
Fruit is produced by multinational corporations only
Prices of fruit are fixed by the WTO

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Foreign trade is integrating markets in different countries. Producers reach buyers beyond their own country, and buyers get goods from abroad: markets are being connected (integrated) through trade. Bans would stop this, fruit is grown by many farmers, and the WTO does not fix prices.

questions.stem_md: A shopper in Kochi can choose among phones from Indian, Korean, Chinese and American brands at similar prices. Which feature of globalisation does this mainly reflect?

options.text_md: Restriction of imports through high taxes
Movement of people from India to Korea
Nationalisation of the phone industry
Integration of markets, giving consumers wider choice

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Integration of markets, giving consumers wider choice. When markets are connected, goods from many countries are sold side by side, so buyers get more choice. High taxes would reduce choice; migration and nationalisation are not involved.

questions.stem_md: Why do MNCs usually set up production where they can get cheap labour and other resources, and also be close to markets?

options.text_md: Because governments force all companies to move abroad
To lower their costs of production and earn greater profits
To reduce the number of goods they sell
Because they are not allowed to make profits in their home country

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** To lower their costs of production and earn greater profits. MNCs choose locations that cut costs (cheap labour, resources) and give access to buyers, so that profits rise. Governments do not force them, they want to sell more, not less, and profits are allowed at home too.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is **NOT** an example of globalisation?

options.text_md: A farmer in Haryana sells wheat at the local mandi in Karnal
A software firm in Bengaluru writes programs for a bank in Germany
A Japanese car company builds a factory in Gujarat
A student in Kolkata takes an online course taught from Canada

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A farmer in Haryana sells wheat at the local mandi in Karnal. Selling wheat at a local market involves no other country. The other three link India with other countries through services trade, foreign investment and technology.

Choose the correct option.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R is about trade in goods and does not explain A. A is explained by visa and immigration restrictions.

questions.solution_md: Definition, then any two of trade, investment, technology, people.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Globalisation** means countries becoming **rapidly integrated**, or interconnected, with one another.
2. Countries connect through **trade in goods and services** and **foreign investment** (also technology and movement of people).

questions.stem_md: What is a multinational corporation? Give one reason why MNCs set up production in other countries.
questions.solution_md: Definition, then one cost or market reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. An **MNC** is a company that **owns or controls production** in **more than one country**.
2. MNCs set up production where they get **cheap labour and resources** and are **close to markets**, which lowers costs and raises **profits**.

questions.stem_md: How does foreign trade lead to integration of markets across countries?
questions.solution_md: Two sides: sellers reach foreign buyers; buyers get foreign goods, so markets join.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Producers can sell **beyond their domestic markets**, competing with producers in other countries.
2. Buyers get **goods produced abroad**, so the **same goods** are sold in many countries at **similar prices**: markets become connected.

questions.stem_md: Why has the movement of people between countries been more limited than the movement of goods?
questions.solution_md: Restrictions on people, compared with liberalised trade and investment.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Countries control entry through **visas, work permits and immigration rules**, often to protect **jobs** for their own citizens.
2. Goods and investment face **far fewer restrictions** today, so they move more freely than people.

questions.stem_md: Explain, with an Indian example of each, three ways in which India is connected to other countries through globalisation.
questions.solution_md: Three channels, each with a concrete Indian example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Trade:** India exports **medicines and software services** and imports **crude oil and electronics**.
2. **Investment:** foreign companies have built **car and phone factories** in Tamil Nadu and Gujarat.
3. **Technology and people:** Indian hospitals use **imported machines and software**, and many Indian **nurses and engineers** work abroad.

marking_scheme.step: Technology or people with an example

questions.stem_md: Explain the role of MNCs in the globalisation process.
questions.solution_md: Three roles: investment, production and trade across borders, technology transfer.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. MNCs **invest** in factories and offices in many countries, moving **capital** across borders.
2. They **spread production** across countries and sell worldwide, so **goods and services** cross borders.
3. They carry **technology and management methods** to the places where they produce, linking the economies of distant countries.

questions.stem_md: What is globalisation? Explain the different ways in which it connects countries, with examples.
questions.solution_md: Definition, then four channels each with an example, noting that people move least.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Meaning:** globalisation is the **rapid integration** or interconnection of countries.
2. **Trade:** more goods and services cross borders; e.g. Indian **mangoes** in London and New Zealand **kiwis** in Pune, so **markets are integrated**.
3. **Investment:** **MNCs** invest in factories and offices abroad; e.g. foreign firms assemble **smartphones** in Tamil Nadu.
4. **Technology:** machines, software and know-how move between countries; e.g. Indian firms provide **IT services** to banks abroad.
5. **People:** people move for work and study, but **less freely** because of visas and immigration rules.

questions.stem_md: "MNCs are the main drivers of globalisation." Do you agree? Give reasons for your answer.
questions.solution_md: Take a position, give three or four roles of MNCs with reasons, and weigh them against the enabling factors.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Largely agree.** MNCs **invest** in many countries, so **capital** moves across borders on a large scale.
2. They **spread production** (design in one country, parts in another, assembly in a third), linking economies.
3. They **sell worldwide**, so **trade** and competition between markets grow.
4. They carry **technology** and management methods to the countries where they produce.
5. **But not alone:** MNCs could do this only because **technology** (containers, internet) made it cheap and **governments liberalised** trade and investment, guided by **WTO rules**; so MNCs drive globalisation, but within conditions others created.

questions.stem_md: Which development in transport has greatly lowered the cost of moving goods across countries?

options.text_md: Bullock carts with rubber tyres
Toll booths on national highways
Containers that are loaded intact onto ships, trains, planes and trucks
Ration cards for transport workers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Containers that are loaded intact onto ships, trains, planes and trucks. Goods packed in standard containers move between trucks, trains and ships without repacking, which cuts handling time and cost. The other options have nothing to do with international transport costs.

questions.stem_md: An animation studio in Kochi colours the pages of a comic book for a publisher in Tokyo and sends the files over the internet the same evening. Which factor of globalisation makes this possible?

options.text_md: Trade barriers
Import quotas
Movement of people
Information and communication technology

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Information and communication technology. Computers, the internet and fast telecommunication let services be produced in one country and delivered instantly to another. Barriers and quotas restrict trade, and nobody travelled.

questions.stem_md: A tax on imports is an example of

options.text_md: foreign investment
liberalisation
a multinational corporation
a trade barrier

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a trade barrier. A tax on imports (a tariff) restricts foreign trade, so it is a trade barrier. Liberalisation means removing such barriers.

questions.stem_md: **Liberalisation** means

options.text_md: putting higher taxes on imported goods
banning foreign companies from investing
removing barriers or restrictions set by the government on trade and investment
the government buying all private factories

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** removing barriers or restrictions set by the government on trade and investment. Liberalisation removes government restrictions so that trade and investment can flow more freely. The other options add restrictions or change ownership.

questions.stem_md: Why did the Indian government put barriers on foreign trade and foreign investment after independence?

options.text_md: To help foreign companies sell more in India
To protect producers within the country, whose industries had only just started, from foreign competition
Because the WTO required all new countries to do so
To increase the prices that foreign buyers paid for Indian goods

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** To protect producers within the country, whose industries had only just started, from foreign competition. Young Indian industries needed protection from established foreign competitors. The barriers did the opposite of helping foreign firms, the WTO did not exist then (it was set up in 1995), and import barriers do not raise prices for foreign buyers.

questions.stem_md: In which year did India make far-reaching changes to remove barriers on foreign trade and investment?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 1991. From 1991, the government decided that Indian producers should compete with producers around the world and removed barriers to a large extent.

questions.stem_md: The main aim of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) is to

options.text_md: give loans to farmers in poor countries
liberalise international trade by setting rules for it
fix the prices of all goods sold in the world
run multinational corporations

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** liberalise international trade by setting rules for it. The WTO sets rules for international trade and aims to make it freer. It does not give farm loans, fix prices or run companies.

questions.stem_md: Developing countries often say that WTO rules work unfairly in practice. Which of the following best supports their view?

options.text_md: Developing countries are not allowed to join the WTO
The WTO bans all exports from developing countries
The WTO requires every country to use the same currency
Some developed countries give large subsidies to their own farmers while asking developing countries to remove protection

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Some developed countries give large subsidies to their own farmers while asking developing countries to remove protection. Large farm subsidies keep prices low for rich countries' farmers and hurt farmers elsewhere, while poorer countries are pressed to open up. Developing countries are members, exports are not banned, and there is no common currency.

questions.stem_md: An imagined country allows only 10,000 tonnes of edible oil to be imported in a year, whatever the price. This is an example of

options.text_md: a quota, a kind of trade barrier
liberalisation of trade
foreign investment
a free-trade rule of the WTO

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a quota, a kind of trade barrier. A limit on the quantity that may be imported is a quota, which restricts trade. It is the opposite of liberalisation and has nothing to do with investment.

questions.stem_md: Which of these services could be provided to a customer abroad **mainly because of** modern information technology?

options.text_md: A barber in Lucknow cutting a tourist's hair
A tailor in Jaipur stitching a dress for a local customer
A Pune firm keeping the accounts of a company in Canada
A taxi driver in Goa taking visitors to the beach

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A Pune firm keeping the accounts of a company in Canada. Accounting can be done remotely and sent over the internet, so the customer can be in another country. The other services need the customer to be physically present.

questions.stem_md: If an imagined country cuts its import duty on bicycles from 40% to 5%, what is the **most likely** immediate effect?

options.text_md: Imported bicycles become more expensive
Local bicycle makers no longer have any competition
Imported bicycles become cheaper, and local makers face more competition
Bicycles can no longer be imported

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Imported bicycles become cheaper, and local makers face more competition. A lower tax on imports lowers their price in the local market, so local producers must compete harder. The other options reverse the effect.

II. Trade barriers make it easier to import goods.

questions.stem_md: In recent years India has signed trade agreements with the UAE, Australia and the United Kingdom that lower import duties on many goods between the partners. These agreements are an example of

options.text_md: putting up new trade barriers
nationalisation
the movement of people only
liberalisation of foreign trade

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** liberalisation of foreign trade. Lowering duties between partners removes barriers to trade, which is liberalisation. It is the opposite of new barriers and has nothing to do with nationalisation.

questions.stem_md: Explain the factors that have enabled globalisation.
questions.solution_md: Two technology factors, two policy points (general and India), and the WTO with its criticism.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Transport technology:** **containers**, bigger ships and cheaper air transport lowered the **cost and time** of moving goods.
2. **Information and communication technology:** **computers, the internet and mobile phones** let firms coordinate production and deliver **services** across countries.
3. **Liberalisation:** governments **removed barriers** such as import taxes and limits, so goods and investment move freely.
4. **India from 1991:** barriers were removed to a large extent so that Indian producers could **compete globally**.
5. **WTO:** its **rules** aim to **liberalise international trade**, though developing countries say developed countries keep **unfair barriers**.

questions.stem_md: Was the removal of trade barriers in India from 1991 a wise decision? Evaluate with reasons.
questions.solution_md: Context, two gains, one cost, and a balanced judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Why barriers existed:** after independence, they protected **young Indian industries** from foreign competition.
2. **Gains:** liberalisation brought **imports of machines and inputs**, more **foreign investment** and **wider choice** for consumers.
3. **Gains (2):** competition pushed many Indian firms to improve **quality**; some became **global companies** themselves.
4. **Costs:** many **small producers** could not match cheaper imports and lost business or closed.
5. **Judgement:** **largely wise**, because India gained growth and choice, but it needed **support for small producers** and fair rules to share the gains.
